full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an order dated 20-4-67 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi, refusing to entertain an appeal preferred against the order of the learned Munsif, Nawabganj, passed in connection with Misc, Care No. 100 of 1965 dismissing an application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for default. 

 2. The petitioner filed a Money Suit in the Court of the Munsif at Nawabganj against the opposite-party for compensation for malicious prosecution. The suit was contested by the opposite-party by filing a written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint. Thereafter 23-6-65 was fixed for peremptory hearing of the said suit which was however, dismissed for default due to non-appearance of the plaintiff on that date. The petitioner thereafter filed an application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Civil Procedure Cede being Miscellaneous Case No. 100 of 1965 praying for setting aside the dismissal order and showing cause for his non-appearance when the suit was called for hearing. The said Misc. Case was fixed for hearing on 7-1-66. The petitioner filed an application for shifting the date of hearing on the ground stated in the said petition. The learned Munsif, however, rejected the petition for time and directed the petitioner to get ready by 10-30 A.M. Thereafter no steps were taken by the petitioner and the learned Munsif dismissed Misc. Case for default by his order dated - 7-1-66. Against the said order the petitioner preferred an appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 52 of 1966 in the Court of the District Judge, Rajshahi, who transferred the same to the learned Subordinate. Judge Rajshahi for disposal 

 (c) an order under rule 9 of Order 9 reacting all application (in a Case open to appeal) for an order to set aside the dismissal of a suit." 

 The learned Subordinate Judge has held that an appeal lies against an order dismissing on merit an application made under Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. but he has stated that no appeal lies when the said dismissal is for default. No such distinction can be read in the aforesaid provisions of Order 43, rule 1(c). Whether the application was dismissed on merit or for default, it is shall the same an order rejecting an application for an order to set aside the dismissal of the suit and for which there is specific provision of appeal under Order 43, rule 1(c). I, therefore, find no reason to restrict an order under Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. to one pass on merit only. This view gets support from a decision in the case of Paidipati Kamma Naraswayya Vs. D. Thimmappa and another, reported in A.I.R. 1943 Madras 584. In the said case a suit was dismissed for default by a Munsif and an application to set aside the dismissal for default was also dismissed for default. Against that order an appeal was preferred by the plaintiff before the District Judge who dismissed the appeal holding that no appeal lies against such order. It was held in that case that an order dismissing for default an application under Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. is appealable under Order 43, rule 1(c) C.P.C. It was further held that there was no reason to confine an order passed on an application under Order 9, rule 9 to one passed on merit only. Similar view has been taken in the case of Uma Dutta Vs, Mt. Zakia Bibi reported in A.I.R. 1936 Allahabad 737. The wording of clause (c) and (d) of rule 1 of Order 43 are almost the same, the only difference being that one clause deals with the dismissal of a suit and the other with a decree passed exparte. The principles laid down in the cases dealing with clause (d) of Tile 1 of Order 43 Cr.P.C. may therefore equally apply to the present case some of the decisions under the said Clause (d) may profitably be considered. In the case of Kumud Kumar Bose and others Vs. Hari Mohan Samaddar, reported in 21 C.L.J. 628, the District Judge has refused to entertain an appeal against an order by which the Court of first instance dismissed for default an application to set aside an exparte decree in a Mortgage Suit. The petitioner who was the defendant in that suit applied to have the exparte decree set aside, ultimately the said application was dismissed for default. On appeal the District Judge passed the following Order:- 

 "No appeal lies, Summarily dismissed." It was held by the Calcutta High Court in that case that under clause (d) of rule 1 of Order 43 of the Code of Civil Procedure the appeal was competent. It was further held that the order assailed by way of appeal was an order under rule 13 of Order 9 and it was immaterial that the application to set aside the exparte decree had been dismissed not on the merits but for default, and in that view of the matter the High Court set aside the order of the District Judge. Similar view was taken in the case of Ansar Ali Vs. Bhim Sankar Datta, reported in A.I.R. 1929 Calcutta 407 and in the case of Mufti Reazuddin Vs. Lala Maheshanand, reported in A.I.R. 1929 Patna 529, and in the case of Abdur Rahman Miji and another Vs. Abdul Wadud Mia and another, reported in 2 P.L.R. Dacca 287. Similar view was also taken in a Full Bench case reported in A.I.R. 1954 Assam 1, Madanlall Agarwalla Vs. Tripura Modern Bank Ltd. where the majority view was that under Order 43, rule 1(d) appeal lies when an application under order 9, rule 13 is rejected either on merit or for default and it was observed that there was no justification for taking such a narrow view of the clause and for reading into it words which are nonexistent. In another Full Bench decision in the case of Doma Chowdhury and others Vs. Ram Naresh Lal and others reported in A.I.R. 1959 Patna 121, it was held that an appeal lies under Order 43, rule 1(c) or (d) from an order rejecting for default an application under rule 9 or rule 13 of Order 9 respectively, because on a plain reading of clauses (c) and (d) of rule 1, Order 43, there is no ground for discrimination between rejection of an application on merits and its rejection for default. 

 7. Mr. Md. Mokhtar Hossain, the learned Advocate, appearing for the Opposite-party tried to support the order of the learned Subordinate Judge submitting that the expression rejecting an application under the clauses (c) and (d) of Order 43, rule 1 of the Code is not the same thing as an order dismissing for default an application, under rules 9 and rule 13 respectively of Order 9 of the Code. In support of the contention he relied on a decision in the case of Bajit Lal Pathak Vs. Maharajadhiraj Sir Rameshwar Singh Bahadur, reported in I.L.R. Patna 333. In that case it was held that an order dismissing for default an application to set aside the dismissal of a suit tinder Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. is not covered by order 43, rule 1(c) of the Code and therefore is not appealable. He has cited some other decisions which have, however, no relevancy in the present case in as much as those relates to rejection of a second application for default. The aforesaid Patna case (I.L.R. M-333) has been expressly dissented hem by the same High Court in the case reported in I.L.R. 8 Patna 533 corresponding to A.I.R. 1929 Patna 529 Mufti Reazuddin Vs. Lala Maheshanand, and they followed the Calcutta decision reported in 21 C.I.J. 628. Subsequently the said case (I.L.R. 7 Patna 333) has been overruled by a Full Bench of that Court in the case of Duma Choudhury and others Vs. Ram Naresh Lal and others, reported in A.I.R. 1959 Patna 121. I respectfully agree with the views expressed in the aforesaid decisions wherein it has been held that an appeal lies to the District Judge under Order 43, rule 1(c) C.P.C. against an order of the learned Munsif dismissing for default an application under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code.
